title: GPU pool autoscale tuning and synthetic hammer-test notes
summary: Notes from a mid-quarter investigation into recurring late-evening GPU pool throughput drops. Contains hypotheses about autoscaler configuration, a reproducible synthetic hammer test plan, and a first-pass runbook for oncall mitigation and longer-term fixes.
impact: Intermittent increased tail latency (p95->p99) for Dedicated capacity tenants during peak bursts, several 503s for small batch workloads. Impact window typically 20-45 minutes, sporadic, mostly observed between 22:00-02:00 UTC over 3 weeks.
symptoms_observed:
- Elevated request queue length in gateway (backlog metric +40%)
- Sudden drop in effective GPU utilization on many nodes while a subset hit 100%
- Autoscaler not triggering additional nodes for 8-12 minutes after sustained queue growth
- Increased token latency and request timeouts for small-batch (<64 tokens) workloads
- Pod restarts correlated with OOMKilled messages in a small number of tenants
timeline:
- 2025-10-18: First night of alerts showing p99 token latency spikes
- 2025-10-19..2025-11-02: Irregular occurrences; manual throttles applied to heavy tenants as mitigation
- 2025-11-03: Rafael ran initial flamegraph to rule out model regressions
- 2025-11-04: This document started (initial hypothesis + test plan)
- 2026-01-12: Temporary metric change deployed (scaling_metric -> gpu_utilization) which changed signal smoothing behavior
- 2026-02-07: Two large incidents; triggered deeper investigation and this updated runbook
initial_hypotheses:
1) Autoscaler smoothing window too long and using an averaged GPU metric that hides short bursts.
2) Noisy tenant(s) producing many small concurrent requests, causing OOM fragmentation and eviction cascades.
3) Batching behavior: small requests defeat batching heuristics, producing many short-lived sessions that saturate loading/driver contexts.
4) Scheduling placement causes uneven packing (affinity rules + binpacking) leading to hot nodes and underutilized nodes elsewhere.
observability_queries_used:
PromQL examples we used in the hunt:
- gateway_backlog_total: sum(rate(gateway_request_queue_length[1m])) by (pool)
- gpu_utilization: avg(nvidia_gpu_utilization_percent) by (node)
- per_node_gpu_mem_free: avg(nvidia_gpu_memory_free_bytes) by (node)
- pod_batch_size_hist: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_batch_size_bucket[5m])) by (le, tenant))
- pod_ooms: increase(kube_pod_container_status_last_terminated_reason{reason=~"OOMKilled"}[30m])
Notes: pay attention to choice of range vector (1m vs 5m) — too wide hides short spikes.
runbook_draft_oncall:
Step 0: Triage (first 10 minutes)
- Confirm alerts: p99 latency > baseline AND gateway_queue_len > baseline
- Open incident channel and post initial snapshot (links to grafana panels)

Step 1: Rapid containment (10-20 minutes)
- Identify candidate noisy tenants: inspect top-5 tenants by request rate over last 5m (use :rate queries).
- If a single tenant is > 50% of requests: apply soft throttle via rate-limit header (example):
  curl -X POST "https://controlplane.redwood/api/tenants/<TENANT>/throttle" -d '{"rate": 200}'
- If noisy tenant is unknown or multiple tenants: scale up emergency burst capacity (manual override) by +2 nodes for the pool:
  kubectl -n dedicated patch scalecfg <pool-scaler> --type=merge -p '{"spec":{"desiredCapacityOverride": <current> + 2}}'
  (note: this is provisional — see infra playbook for exact command for our autoscaler operator)

Step 2: Isolation (20-40 minutes)
- Cordon hot nodes and drain low-priority pod classes: kubectl cordon <node>; kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data --force
- Annotate suspected tenant's pods to move them to a dedicated pool if annotated routing is enabled: kubectl annotate pod <pod> redwood/force-dedicated=true
- If memory fragmentation observed (OOMKilled logs), temporarily lower per-tenant concurrency via config: set CONCURRENCY_LIMIT=2 for that tenant via controlplane API

Step 3: Recovery verification (40-60 minutes)
- Check that gateway queue returns to baseline and p99 latency drops. If not, escalate to infra oncall to inspect node-level GPU driver logs and perform node reboot if necessary.

Step 4: Post-incident capture
- Record timeline, commands executed, and attach graphs and logs to JIRA ticket JIRA-ENG-5423
- Create follow-up action items (see follow_up_actions) and assign owners
emergency_mitigations_examples:
- Manual scale override (+ nodes)
- Tenant soft-throttle via rate-limiter
- Move heavy tenant to reserved/dedicated pool if available
- Temporary increase of autoscaler aggressiveness (reduce cooldown to 30s) — only if safe and paired with surge budget
- Drain and reboot a node if driver-level throttling suspected
synthetic_hammer_test_plan:
Purpose: reproduce late-evening burst profile and validate autoscaler response + fairness controls
Overview: run a distributed load generator that emits many small requests with realistic token lengths and inter-arrival distribution (poisson + occasional spikes)
Test bed: non-prod Dedicated GPU pool (staging-dedicated-3) with same autoscaler config as prod
Load profile: 3 phases
- Warmup (5m): ramp to 30% aggregated GPU utilization with medium sized requests (256 tokens)
- Hammer (15m): emit high QPS of small requests (1-2 tokens, batch size 1-4) from 50 simulated tenants; introduce a heavy tenant that represents 60% of QPS for 5 minutes
- Recovery (10m): drop load and observe autoscaler cooldown and pooling behaviour
Measurement goals:
- Time-to-scale: time for autoscaler to add nodes to bring avg gpu_utilization under 70%
- Fairness: percent of small requests that see increased latency when heavy tenant is active
- Pod churn: number of pod restarts and OOMs during test
Tools and commands:
- Use siege-like generator wrapped in a k8s job that authenticates as simulated tenants
- Example runner: python loadgen/runner.py --tenants 50 --profile hammer --duration 1800 --target pool=staging-dedicated-3
- Collect telemetry: ensure prometheus scrape rate at 15s, record raw driver metrics and dmesg from nodes
test_observability_targets: - Ensure dashboards show both 1m and 5m resolution panels\n- Add temporary histogram for request latency by tenant\n- Capture node-level nvml logs (nvmlEvent log) for entire test window
longer_term_recommendations:
1) Change autoscaler signal to short-window percentile (e.g., 95th of 1m samples) instead of long moving average.
2) Implement tenant-level rate budgeting and fair-queueing to avoid single-tenant hog.
3) Improve placement constraints to prefer even GPU packing across nodes when bursty workloads forecasted.
4) Add surge capacity pool that can be spun up faster (warm standby nodes).
5) Add a chaos test to CI that runs the synthetic hammer once per release to catch regressions.
6) Revisit default concurrency settings and batching heuristics for small-batch opt-in clients.
monitoring_changes_proposed:
- New alerts:
  * gpu_pool_sustained_backlog (5m backlog > threshold)
  * per_tenant_request_skew (top-tenant > 50% of requests over 5m)
  * node_gpu_fragmentation_indicator (increase in memory_free variance across GPUs)
- Dashboards:
  * add tenant-by-tenant latency heatmap
  * add synthetic-hammer playback panel with expected vs actual scale response
- Logging:
  * persist container driver logs to centralized objstore for 48h when threshold crossed

notes_to_self: - When running the hammer test in staging, watch for hidden differences: node SKU placement and image versions.\n- If we make autoscaler more aggressive, throttle the rate of node creation to avoid cloud provider quota surprises.\n- Consider adding an experiment tag to the test traffic so it is excluded from customer analytics.

decision_log: - Keep default batching heuristics for now but expose per-tenant override flag (agreed: 2026-02-08)\n- Short-window metric change approved for staging only for initial validation (agreed: 2026-02-09)\n- No immediate change to tenancy allocation policy until synthetic tests complete (agreed: 2026-02-10)
